title: Which family office problems can AI fix first?
description: For family office COOs: five problems AI helps with first, ranked by peer surveys, from the manual quarterly report to comparing fund managers.
verdict: Five problems fill a family office's week: the quarterly report, fund documents, partnership books, comparing managers and the deadline calendar.[^34][^35]
The quarterly report hurts most: 73% of 155 North American family offices call investment reporting too manual, three years running.[^34][^1]
Fund documents feed it: the average private markets investment sends 13 a year, in waves after quarter end.[^35][^36]
Comparing managers before committing strains small teams: 41% of investors in one due diligence survey lack time to finish reviews.[^37][^4]
AI reads and matches; your people keep every sign-off, payment and fund commitment.[^13][^14]

summary: AI for family offices reads fund documents, matches them to the books and drafts reports, so staff check instead of key.[^13][^5] Most offices want a leaner office, not better returns, and privacy comes first.[^5][^12] Clean data plumbing and a person who signs off make or break it.[^6][^13]
humanRole: Your controller signs off before anything AI extracts reaches the general ledger or the reporting system. Review AI output before it enters a system of record.[^6][^16][^13]

A person reviews, authorizes and releases every payment, even when AI queues the bill.[^14] In one vendor's statement workflow (Risclarity, writing for FOX), an analyst reviews and maps AI-read data before import.[^16]
Investment, tax, legal and family decisions stay with qualified professionals. AI output informs them and a professional reviews it.[^12][^5]
The COO owns the AI policy and the list of approved tools. Offices Simple interviewed put policy first, then approved tools, data segmentation and human review.[^6][^26]

The investment committee keeps the vote on every fund commitment, and AI only lines up the managers' answers.[^37][^42] Keep a decision log with the source behind each point, because AI prompts and logs may be discoverable records.[^15][^17]

ranked.name: The quarterly report is too manual
ranked.why: 73% of 155 North American family offices say investment reporting is too manual, a top concern three years running.[^34] 72% of family offices use or pilot AI for reporting automation.[^1]
ranked.payoff: Days from quarter end to the family's report, and hours keyed per report.

ranked.name: Fund documents flood in every quarter
ranked.why: The average private markets investment sends 13 documents a year, and the top decile 25 or more, by Arch's platform data.[^35] In a vendor's poll of 70+ family offices, collecting documents was the top challenge, at 36%.[^36]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per document from portal to filed, and documents still keyed by hand.

ranked.name: The books lag the capital calls and K-1s
ranked.why: Family offices spend 20% of working hours on manual tasks, up to 40% in larger offices, in a sponsored survey of 44 offices.[^38] One New York family office posted a senior controller role whose duties start with capital calls and K-1 support.[^33]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per notice from inbox to booked entry, and days to close each entity.

ranked.name: Comparing fund managers takes too long
ranked.why: 41% of 44 investors in an operational due diligence survey say they lack time to finish reviews, and family offices were among them.[^37] 39% of family offices use or plan to use AI for investment due diligence.[^41]
ranked.payoff: Weeks from the first questionnaire to the committee memo, and answers checked against evidence.

ranked.name: Something is always due
ranked.why: Partnership K-1s are due by the 15th day of the third month after year end, and an extension adds six months.[^39] By our count, a model 30-filer office faces 159 filing deadlines a year.[^40]
ranked.payoff: Deadlines met without a scramble, and hours spent chasing documents.

ranked.name: Choosing the software that fixes each problem
ranked.why: The average family office tech stack costs $100,000 to $500,000 a year, per Campden Wealth and AlTi Tiedemann.[^11] Most AI features are narrow and tied to one platform, so the stack decides what AI can reach.[^13]
ranked.payoff: Manual re-keys between systems each month, and reports built from one data set.

ranked.name: The operating companies the family owns
ranked.why: 77% of families UBS surveyed have an active operating business.[^8] 67% hold controlling stakes, so the office often sets the companies' reporting and close.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Days to roll the companies into the family's balance sheet.

ownData.title: What are your peers hiring for?
ownData.intro: We read 26 US family office job postings by hand on 28 Nov 2026, and tallied the work each one names.[^29] Ten name AI or automation, mostly controller, finance-head and analytics roles.[^29][^31][^30] Entities or consolidation lead the duties at 11 of 26, then reconciliation and reporting at 8 each.[^29]

ownData.note: Zavient hand-read of 26 US family office postings dated Sep 2025 to Nov 2026, read 28 Nov 2026 on each original page.[^29] A duty counts only if named; pay is the median of posted-range midpoints, with pay-site estimates left out.[^33] Limits: small, hand-read, US-only and not random; many are recruiter posts, and two New York tech posts may be one role.

rules.name: SEC family office rule, 17 CFR 275.202(a)(11)(G)-1
rules.what: An office is not an investment adviser if it serves only family clients, is family-owned and controlled, and doesn't hold itself out as one.[^18][^19] The rule says nothing about AI, so your own policy sets the bar.

rules.name: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Regulation S-P amendments
rules.status: Compliance from 3 Dec 2025 (larger firms) and 3 Jun 2026 (smaller)
rules.what: These apply to SEC-registered advisers, such as a multi-family office that registers.[^20] You need an incident response program, customer notice within 30 days, and vendors who report breaches within 72 hours.[^20][^21] Any AI vendor that touches client data falls under that oversight.

rules.name: Form 13F
rules.status: In force; due within 45 days of each quarter end
rules.what: An office with $100 million or more in Section 13(f) securities files Form 13F, family office or not.[^22][^23] AI can draft the holdings list, and a person checks it before filing.

rules.name: FinCEN beneficial ownership reporting
rules.status: US companies exempt; final rule effective 14 Aug 2026
rules.what: US entities no longer file beneficial ownership reports with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).[^24][^25] Keep your own entity register current anyway, because AI that books by entity is only as good as that list.

rules.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
rules.status: Voluntary; version 1.0 from Jan 2023, under revision
rules.what: A free, voluntary frame for writing your AI policy, with a separate profile for generative AI.[^26] It is guidance, not law, so adopt what fits an office of your size.

watchOuts: Family data in public chatbots: RSM warns against putting confidential reports into public ChatGPT.[^13] Give staff one approved tool, and ask each vendor whether it trains on your data.[^6][^13]
Voice-cloned wire requests: business email compromise drew $3,046,598,558 in reported losses in 2025.[^27] Agree a secret phrase with the family, and call back on a known number before any wire.[^28]

Extraction errors that reach the books: an AI misread on a capital call or K-1 flows into every report after it. Risclarity, a vendor writing for FOX, has analysts review and map output before import into the system of record.[^16]
Logs nobody planned for: AI prompts and logs may be discoverable records.[^15] Set retention rules and keep a decision log before staff use AI on trust or investment work.
Builds only one person understands: Simple's 2026 report finds in-house builds tend to break on data plumbing and on dependence on one key person.[^6] Document each build and give it a second owner.
No measured payoff: 24% of offices see no measurable impact from AI, and 31% of smaller offices.[^3] Pick one workflow and one before-and-after number before you start.

faq.q: Is it safe to put family data into AI tools?
faq.a: Only in approved tools that keep your data out of model training and inside your office's controls.[^13] Offices Simple interviewed name approved tools, data segmentation and running models locally as their controls.[^6]

faq.q: Where should a family office start with AI?
faq.a: Start with the problem that eats the most hours, usually the quarterly report or fund document intake.[^34][^6] PwC sets guidelines and training in the first 3 months, then scales proven workflows over 3 to 12 months.[^12]

faq.q: Can AI compare fund managers for us?
faq.a: Only as a first pass: AI can line up each manager's questionnaire answers, but people must check them.[^37][^42] The Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) says yes/no answers give only a top-level view, never the sole basis for a decision.[^42]

faq.q: Do we need to hire an AI person?
faq.a: Not usually, because offices add AI duties to finance and operations roles: 10 of 26 postings we read ask for it.[^29] Only one was an AI engineer.[^32] Lack of internal expertise is still the top barrier, named by 57% of family offices.[^4]

faq.q: Does the SEC regulate how a family office uses AI?
faq.a: No, not with an AI-specific rule: an office that meets the family office exclusion is not an investment adviser.[^18] A multi-family office that registers as an adviser falls under Regulation S-P's data rules.[^20]

faq.q: Do AI chats and notes become records we may have to produce?
faq.a: Yes, they can: Northern Trust warns that AI prompts and logs may be discoverable records.[^15] Set retention rules before staff use AI for trust or investment work.

faq.q: What does AI cost a family office?
faq.a: No standard price exists: the average technology stack AI runs on costs $100,000 to $500,000 a year, per Campden Wealth and AlTi Tiedemann.[^11] For scale, IT is 7% of the average office's pure cost.[^7]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy the plumbing: reporting, aggregation and accounting platforms are standard, and vendors warn offices against building their own system of record.[^6] About four in ten offices already use third-party consolidated reporting software.[^4]
buyVsBuild.build: Build the views and workflows that are yours, such as your entities, reports and privacy rules; Simple calls it buy the plumbing, build the view.[^6] Offices keep work in-house for expertise (67%), privacy (63%) and control (63%).[^7] RSM describes three shapes: a data warehouse, agents, or a hybrid.[^13]

pickElse: Your reporting platform, such as Addepar or Canoe, already has the AI feature you need: use it first. Most AI features are tied to one platform.[^13]
The gap is cybersecurity, not workflow: buy a managed security service. 38% of single family offices fully outsource cybersecurity.[^9]
The problem is data plumbing, not judgment: a vendor's managed data operations may fit. Offices already hand IT to outside providers.[^6]
You run a registered multi-family office: start from our wealth management guide, since Regulation S-P applies to registered advisers.[^20]

sources.name: BNY Wealth, Are Family Offices Really Using AI?, 5 Nov 2026
sources.what: Survey of 290 family offices (N from BNY's companion page, How Family Offices Invest Today): 8% of respondents say AI is extensively integrated into investment decision-making, 29% partially integrated, 40% experimental. Using or piloting AI: reporting automation 72%, portfolio analytics 70%, investment research 72%, market insights and summarization 71%, risk 69%, idea generation 60%, cash management 49%, tax and estate planning 46%. 61% say AI improved investment outcomes; 4% report a negative impact.

sources.name: BNY Wealth, How Family Offices Invest Today
sources.what: Companion page to BNY's AI findings. Survey of 290 family offices: the research polled key decision-makers at 290 family offices.

sources.name: Citi Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report, 18 Sep 2026
sources.what: Survey of 351 family offices in more than 40 countries. AI maturity: 40% early adoption, 30% moderate, 10% advanced, 2% transformational, 19% none. AI uses: AI-generated meeting notes 38%, knowledge management 32%, document management 30%. 24% see no measurable impact (31% of smaller offices vs 19% of larger). 67% own controlling stakes in operating businesses.

sources.name: Citi Private Bank, 2025 Global Family Office Report
sources.what: Survey of 346 family offices. Barriers to technology adoption: lack of internal expertise 57%, lack of awareness 34% (42% at smaller offices), cybersecurity or privacy concerns 28%, return-on-investment uncertainty 25%; only 48% felt cybersecurity was well managed. Technology priorities: investment and data analytics platforms 50%, consolidated reporting 39%, cybersecurity 37%, AI and machine learning 28%. About four in ten use third-party consolidated reporting software. Of the services family offices get from external investment advisors, due diligence and access to managers is named by 41% of family offices (read 28 Nov 2026).

sources.name: Citi Institute, AI in the Family Office, 11 May 2026
sources.what: For family offices the prime goal of AI is "leanness - not (yet) alpha"; privacy comes first; practical uses are summarizing documents, meeting transcription, email and automating reports. "Humans stay in charge."

sources.name: Simple, Family Office Software & Technology Report 2026, 4 Nov 2026
sources.what: Interviews with 41 family offices (AI came up in 31) and 36 vendors. In offices AI mostly sits at assistant level (55%) vs task level (23%); no autonomous agents seen in offices, while 22% of vendors claim or pilot them. Document intake is a common first target. Some offices still put reporting together by hand; manual reporting and data plumbing named by 32% of offices and 75% of vendors, capacity and implementation by 37% of offices. Privacy concern: 32% of 31 offices vs 39% of vendors; security 46% vs 58%. Controls offices named: policy first, approved tools, data segmentation, traceability, human review, running models locally. "Buy the plumbing, build the view." Simple's table of in-house builds: they tend to break on data plumbing, maintenance and scale, and dependence on one key person; vendors warn against building your own system of record. Offices hand IT to outside providers, but reporting seems to stay in-house; some vendors now sell managed data operations. The only agents heard about in offices were ones the office built itself.

sources.name: UBS, Global Family Office Report 2025
sources.what: Survey of 317 family offices: average staff 12; staff are 67% of pure cost and IT/technology 7%; pure cost averages 41.1 bps. Likely AI uses in the next five years: financial reporting and data visualization 69%, text analysis 64%, portfolio analysis 62%; only 6% expect no AI use. Offices keep work in-house for expertise (67%), privacy (63%) and control (63%).

sources.name: UBS, Global Family Office Report 2026 press release, 28 May 2026
sources.what: Survey of 307 family offices: 77% have an active operating business.

sources.name: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report
sources.what: Survey of 333 single family offices (197 US). Kept wholly in-house: balance-sheet aggregation and reporting 54%, financial administration 64%. 38% outsource cybersecurity wholly, and it is the greatest service need at 32%. 40% spend under $1 million a year to run the office; average operating cost just over $3 million, $6.6 million at $1 billion+. 80% of global family offices report some portfolio outsourcing, such as outsourced CIOs, due diligence and manager selection (read 28 Nov 2026).

sources.name: RBC and Campden Wealth, North America Family Office Report 2025, press release, 16 Oct 2025
sources.what: Survey of 317 family offices (141 North American). North American offices: 29% use generative AI for investment reporting and 63% are interested; automated investment reporting 69%, up from 46%. Manual processes and spreadsheets are top operational risks.

sources.what: Read 28 Nov 2026. Survey of 146 family offices (82 North American). "The average costs range is between US $100,000 to US $500,000 annually" for a family office tech stack. A family office quoted: "There is no way we want our data to be in the hands of someone else."

sources.name: PwC, How AI is Reshaping the Modern Family Office, 8 Jun 2026
sources.what: Value clusters: diligence, reporting and board packs, and knowledge. "Licences don't create value, changed work does." The case is "not so much that of reducing headcount". Any AI output that informs an investment, tax, legal or family decision is reviewed by a qualified professional. Roadmap: first 0-3 months, then 3-12 months.

sources.name: RSM US, AI preparedness for family offices, 1 Oct 2025
sources.what: Five practical uses of AI in family office systems, including wealth aggregation and reporting, document management and CRM. Most AI features remain narrow and tied to a single platform, like automating bill pay, classifying ledger transactions or extracting values from capital call notices. Human judgment remains central; AI use policies should prohibit uploading confidential reports into public models like ChatGPT; ask whether the vendor uses family office data to train its model. Three architectures: data warehouse, agentic, hybrid.

sources.name: EY Canada, How family offices can boost efficiency with AI, 15 Jul 2024
sources.what: AI cues up the payables process so administrators focus on "human in the loop" activities: the review, authorization and release of payments. AI can scan Schedule K-1s and synthesize their information.

sources.what: Keep decision logs and source-traceable reasoning when AI informs trust or investment decisions; AI prompts and logs may be discoverable records.

answers.human-role: Your people keep every decision: the controller signs off what reaches the books, a person releases every payment, and the investment committee votes on every commitment.[^16][^14][^37]
answers.ranked: Hand AI the manual quarterly report first, then the fund-document flood, the lagging books, manager comparison and the deadline calendar, in order of reported pain.[^34][^35][^37]
answers.own-data: Peers mostly hire controllers and finance staff for entity accounting, reconciliation and reporting, and 10 of the 26 postings we read ask for AI or automation.[^29]
answers.table-1: The surveys agree family offices are early: only 8% of 290 say AI is extensively integrated, and most use sits at assistant level.[^1][^6]
answers.table-2: A family office spends most of its budget on people: staff are 67% of pure cost and technology is 7%, per UBS.[^7]
answers.rules: No AI-specific rule applies, but the SEC family office exclusion, Regulation S-P for registered offices and Form 13F shape what AI may touch.[^18][^20][^22]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI goes wrong in a family office when family data leaks into public tools, extraction errors reach the books, or fraudsters clone a voice to move money.[^13][^16][^28]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy the data platform and build the office-specific views on top, the split Simple's 2026 report calls buy the plumbing, build the view.[^6]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when your platform already has the AI feature, the gap is cybersecurity, or the problem is data plumbing rather than judgment.[^13][^9][^6]

offer.heading: Which family office problem should AI take first?
offer.body: Usually the quarterly report or fund document intake. In a free 30-minute call we map one problem end to end. You leave knowing who signs off, the number to track and where family data stays.

reviews.notes: Reads as the office's COO. The ranked jobs and payoff measures are usable. The single all-in operations pay figure skewed the table; labelled it an outlier. Offer gives a clear first step. Reframe pass: the five problems now open the page in the order I feel them; the fund-manager row points to my COO page for now.

Checked each payoff can be measured from today's process. The software-stack payoff was vague; changed to manual re-keys a month and reports from one data set. Human-role bullets name who signs off. Reframe pass: each problem names the page that fixes it, so I can send one link per owner.

Read as the principal's chief of staff in a single family office. The operating-company row and links to holding companies, multi-entity close and private equity carry the business side. No changes. Reframe pass: the holding companies row still routes the operating business to its own playbook. No changes.

Read as the controller. EY backs human release of payments but not a K-1 check, so the K-1 claim was cut; the import review now cites FOX's analyst review before import. Capital call and K-1 work routes to the accounting guide. Reframe pass: the books row now says why they lag, late K-1s and calls, before it says what AI does.

Bottom line reads first and plain: early adoption, reporting first, expertise gap, data stays in the office. Wire-fraud watch-out is the one a principal will act on. No changes. Reframe pass: the investment committee keeps the vote on any fund commitment. No price added.
